## Introduction

We struggle to imagine a society that deals well with powerful AI. We must keep trying, however, because without a positive vision we’re haplessly reacting to the economic and geopolitical consequences. Current proposals, like Dario Amodei’s “ Machines of Loving Grace ,” leave important questions wide open:

- Questions of meaning, purpose, and connection. One consequence of AI agents is that we spend time with them. Do we then spend less with each other? If AIs replace us in the workplace, will we lose some of our social relationships? our sense of purpose? As Clara Collier 1 observed recently, work is where many of us mix with those outside our class or scene, and earn respect for our skills. A new social vision should say how humans can continue to find purpose beyond status games, and mix across social divides.

- Questions of the proper division of labor. As AIs do more work, they’ll also do more decision-making, depriving humans of some kinds of experience, learning, and skill-building. AIs will increasingly draft rules, settle disputes, and interpret whether values are being fulfilled, and may come to exceed humans at some of these tasks. A new social vision must somehow define what humans should still do, and how they will go on learning, growing, and exercising judgement.

- Questions of power and influence. If AIs do more decision-making, how can we ensure that human interests remain central? We currently attempt to keep government aligned with human interests via elections, the rule of law, and other checks and balances, and businesses aligned with consumers via markets. But these are already under strain: government agencies and companies drift away from what they were set up for, and voters and customers often can’t correct it. 2 AI agents can pursue whatever metrics we give them tirelessly and faster than any human. When those metrics don’t capture what we care about, or are gamed, misalignment with human interests grows more severe. A new social vision must therefore explain how humans can retain influence over the institutions that shape their lives.

I’ll present a social vision that addresses these questions, drawing from a strain of political theory called associationalism. 3 Associationalism is the idea that more decisions could be made in associations — groups that people choose to join to pursue some purpose together under rules they agree on, such as churches, unions, cooperatives, or clubs. 4

Below, I will focus on associations that are bound to a purpose and held accountable to it, rather than following whatever their members want at a given moment, and where those purposes can be revised in some ways, but not others, such that the purpose sometimes might outlive the current members’ interest in it. 5 And I will focus more on lightweight associations that are easier to find, form, and leave. Some will be much lighter than a church or a union, such as a pool of buyers who want the same outcome, or a group of parents who share activities among their children for a time. An individual might belong to many.

Associationalism has always had a clear appeal: instead of ceding authority to the “artificial intelligence” of the market’s price mechanism, 6 or to distant state bureaucrats, people in associations, those who share a concern, can make decisions about it themselves. 7

And with these lightweight, purposeful associations, there’s an additional benefit: if associations form easily around new purposes, life can become more purposeful without us all agreeing on any particular one. The upshot is, hopefully, that the kind of “consumer choices” we have today, where we pick among products, can be augmented by a new kind of “values choice,” where we select which purposes we want to be part of.

I’ll call a society where this happens telocratic . 8 Telocracy doesn’t require powerful AI, but it helps a lot: AI can help people form associations who otherwise wouldn’t find each other, 9 and can lower the time cost of being part of an association and a custodian of its purpose. AI can also hold associations accountable to their purposes, interpreting and enforcing them across a wide range of cases, allowing greater trust in these associations and avoiding their capture by sectional interests. 10

I’ll first cover telocracy in broad terms, then offer concrete institutional and legal ideas, including new market structures for group buying and for forming associations, a way to move government work to AI agents that are monitored by purpose, and some more radical ideas, like automatically reallocating assets (such as compute) to align them with purposes.

## Telocracy

I will focus on modern liberal societies, where others have argued we will face acute problems of meaning, division of labor, disempowerment, and power concentration due to AI. 11 Introducing telocracy there means changes like these:

- Telocratic governance . More institutions will have extensively articulated purposes or mandates, kind of like Claude’s Constitution, 12 which can evolve over time in some ways but not others. Unlike bylaws, these focus on the purpose of the institution, not on procedure or what it owes to stakeholders. They can operate at various levels of abstraction — for instance, parents who disagree about educational methods might still agree to a school that tries multiple approaches to learn which work. 13 Legally, these “telocratic” organizations may be companies, government agencies, or nonprofits, but they are more tightly tied to their purposes, via AI-based channels of interpretation and enforcement. These are organizations that have safeguards and monitoring much like those that frontier AI models already have today, but applied to the organization itself. 14

- Purpose-fit groups . In a telocracy, people are assisted in finding and forming groups with a potential shared purpose. AI can help match groups and purposes by varying either: first, purposes can be posed at various levels of abstraction, mentioned above, to find a group which could sustain them; second, populations can be found that match variations on more concrete purposes. Continuing the example of parents and schools, different parent groups can be matched to schools with different approaches. Thus, a greater diversity of purposes can be realized in society. This could raise the ceiling, sustaining more ambitious projects (especially those which don’t fit neatly into state or market provision), and also raise the floor by allowing AIs to help disorganized and disadvantaged groups find each other, based on a common shared purpose, and coordinate. 15

- Moving power around . Many functions, like public schooling, social media, or nursing homes, are controlled by the state or the market, but exist uneasily in either. When public schools are run by the state, this gives power to state officials, who may not be ideal for making those decisions. But if they were instead run by the market, power would instead reside with owners and managers, who also may not be the right people to wield it. The traditional third option is civil society: churches, unions, charities, clubs, and other associations. But for a century or so, liberal societies have let the state and the market absorb much of what these associations used to do. 16 Part of why 17 is that associations were less accountable than state actors, and less dynamic and responsive to people’s needs than market actors. This made associations an overall worse choice for many functions, and so they were crowded out. Telocracy aims to reverse this, by giving associations a new way to be accountable to their purposes (telocratic governance), and creating a kind of automatic entrepreneurialism in this third sector ( purpose-fit groups ). This could give us a new place to put functions we’d like to be dynamic and accountable, such as social media, public schooling, and nursing homes.

### Telocratic Governance

Imagine writing a ten-page constitution for an organization. It describes what the organization is for, what trade-offs are legitimate, and where the boundaries of its mission lie.

Until recently, it would be difficult to know how such a constitution would apply across the thousands of cases the organization might encounter. But AI changes this: a model can be given a natural-language constitution and trained or prompted to apply it across a large space of cases. One can generate thousands of hypothetical situations, including adversarial and boundary cases, and ask which actions the model regards as consistent with the constitution, which it rejects, and which remain uncertain.

Imagine such a constitution isn’t as vague as most current mission statements, but has values spelled out with uncanny precision, detailing which trade-offs are legitimate in operations, and more. (See Appendix A for a precise account of what these purpose documents must contain.)

And imagine this document can change. The purpose can be revised as the organization learns, and it can move between more abstract and more value-laden 18 formulations, depending on how much trust the organization wants to earn. A book club might just have a few sentences about reading hard books whereas a school or hospital might spell out more.

The document can then be applied in many ways: it can monitor internal decision-making, sending alerts when decisions depart from it. It can constrain AI agents acting for the organization. It can supply standards for independent auditors, and provide evidence in external adjudication. It can even be used for external assessment of how the organization delivers on its purpose: if the document claims the organization exists to deliver or protect a particular value, AIs can interview those impacted and see if their experience bears that out.

This new technology could enable big changes in the law, and in how institutions are governed. Western law 19 often assigns governance to specified persons and offices, based on their interests. Think shareholders, members, voters, principals, plaintiffs, and beneficiaries. In each case, the essential question is what some entitled person, member, or constituency may demand. Call this “stakeholder governance.”

In government agencies and large organizations, we find a second kind: “procedural governance.” Here, the question is if the right steps were followed. The hope is for everyone to get the same treatment, with no important considerations skipped.

A third alternative, comparatively less mature, is “telocratic governance.” Its animating question is whether an institution remains faithful to its articulated purpose, which supplies an independent standard to which the institution is held accountable.

In small communities, telocratic governance isn’t new. Benedictine monasteries operate on the Rule of St. Benedict, which, in 73 chapters, describes the purpose of the monastery and how to pursue it. At larger scale, charities, public-benefit corporations, and purpose-specific public bodies offer a primitive form of such governance, 20 but their purposes are usually a sentence or two, and the same people are interpreting them as are supposed to be following them.

A big question for telocratic governance is deciding when these purposes can change. We don’t want institutions ruled by the “dead hand” 21 of their founders, but we also don’t want them captured by current stakeholders. Some principles can guide us: for instance, purposes can bind more tightly once outsiders rely on the institution in various ways ( living commitments ), and bind more loosely when it’s easy for people to walk away.

Even when purposes bind tightly, they should be revisable when the purpose has been achieved, or when it can be better served another way ( legitimate deepening ).
